svg.title: The Log4Shell timeline, from a private report to an endemic vulnerability
svg.desc: A vertical timeline with colored dots: red for disclosure and attacks, green for fixed releases, blue for government actions and catalogs, purple for the review. November 24, 2021: a researcher privately reports the JNDI lookup flaw to Apache. December 5 and 6: the fix is committed and release candidate 2.15.0-rc1 is tagged. December 9: details go public and exploitation attempts begin. December 10: Log4j 2.15.0 is released and CVE-2021-44228 is published with CVSS 10.0, and CISA adds it to the KEV catalog with a due date of December 24. December 13: 2.16.0 removes message lookups. December 14: CVE-2021-45046 shows the 2.15.0 fix was incomplete. December 17: 2.17.0 fixes CVE-2021-45105, a denial of service, and CISA issues Emergency Directive 22-02 for federal agencies. December 27: 2.17.1 fixes CVE-2021-44832. A bracket marks four fixed releases in 17 days. Seven months later, on July 11, 2022, the Cyber Safety Review Board calls Log4j an endemic vulnerability that will remain perhaps a decade or longer.

g.text: Log4Shell: from a private report to an endemic vulnerability
A researcher privately reports the JNDI lookup flaw to Apache
Details go public; exploitation attempts begin
Log4j 2.15.0 released; CVE-2021-44228 published with CVSS 10.0
CISA adds it to KEV with a due date of December 24
2.17.0 fixes CVE-2021-45105, a denial of service
CISA Emergency Directive 22-02 for federal agencies
Cyber Safety Review Board: an endemic vulnerability, "perhaps a decade or longer"
Four upgrades in 17 days: a zero-day response follows the advisory until it settles.
